## Overview

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design in small sections (200-300 words), checking after each section whether it looks right so far.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**
- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**
- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**
- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Break it into sections of 200-300 words
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

## After the Design

**Documentation:**
- Write the validated design to `docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible

## TFC Game UI Layout — Comprehensive Exploration Report

I've thoroughly explored the TFC player view UI implementation. Here's the complete breakdown:

---

### 1. COMPONENT STRUCTURE FOR PLAYER VIEW

**Main Component:** `/Users/dragan/Documents/AI-Boilerplate/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/features/player/player-view.ts`

The player view uses a 4-row vertical grid layout:
- **Row 1 (Header):** Title, stress bar, clocks
- **Row 2 (Turn Banner):** Current turn event title/description
- **Row 3 (Main Content):** Warfare domain board, system status board, role cards in flexbox grid
- **Row 4 (Footer):** Player status, action buttons

**Key Components:**
- `RoleCardComponent` — individual decision/intel cards for each role
- `SystemStatusBoardComponent` — horizontal status strip showing system power/operational state
- `WarfareDomainBoardComponent` — horizontal threat level indicators
- `BriefingOverlayComponent` — startup instructions
- `CompletionOverlayComponent` — end-of-exercise summary
- `LogsDrawerComponent` — side drawer with decision history

---

### 2. HOW "ALL_ADVISORS" MODE DISPLAYS ALL 3 CREW ROLES

**Role Mode Detection** (player-view.ts, lines 81-96):
```typescript
const isMultiRole = computed(() => {
  const role = this.store.playerRole();
  return (
    role === "all_advisors" || role === "solo_player" || role === "all_roles"
  );
});
```

**Card Building Logic** (player-view.ts, lines 108-139):
- **Single-role players** (e.g., CO, individual advisors): See only their own role card
- **"all_advisors"**: See ALL advisor roles as separate cards
- **"solo_player"** and **"all_roles"**: See all scenario roles (CO + advisors)
- **Decision Maker role:** Also sees advisor recommendations below the decision form

**Card Generation** (role-card.types.ts):
- The `buildRoleCards()` function filters roles based on player role
- If `playerRole === "all_advisors"`, all advisor roles are included
- If `playerType === "decision_maker"` (CO), advisor recommendations are rendered in an "Advisor Recs" section

**Role Definition** (scenario-api.service.ts, line 43-47):
```typescript
export interface RoleDef {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  player_type: string;  // "decision_maker" | "advisor"
}
```

---

### 3. EVENTS/INJECTS AND DECISIONS/BLUECARDS DISPLAY PER ROLE

**Event Display:**
- Events are fetched as `EventSnapshot[]` in the store and displayed in the turn banner
- **Role-specific intel:** Each role can see different event description via `roleDescriptions` object
- Only one active event shows at a time in the banner (lines 20-32 of player-view.html)

**Decision Display:**
- Decisions have `target_roles: string[]` — controls which roles see the decision
- Empty `target_roles` = all roles see it
- `activeDecisions` computed filter (lines 76-89 of player-view.ts):
  - Multi-role players (`"all_advisors"`, `"solo_player"`, `"all_roles"`, `"decision_maker"`) see all open decisions
  - Single-role players see only decisions where their role is in `target_roles`

**Decision Question Types:**
- `single_choice` — radio buttons
- `multi_choice` — checkboxes
- `free_text` — textarea input

**Advisor Recommendations** (CO view only):
- When the CO (decision_maker) role is active, they see "Advisor Recommendations" section
- Shows recommendations from each advisor role as they submit
- Pending recommendations show "pending..." until submitted
- Full recommendation list built from `decision.recommendations` object (key: roleId, value: selected optionId)

---

### 4. CSS LAYOUT FOR PLAYER VIEW

**File:** `/Users/dragan/Documents/AI-Boilerplate/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/shared/components-player-view.css`

**Grid Structure:**
```css
.player-layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: auto auto 1fr auto;  /* header | banner | main | footer */
  height: 100dvh;
  overflow: hidden;
}
```

**Main Content Area:**
```css
.player-main--board {
  padding: 0;
  gap: 0;
}
```

**Role Cards Grid (flexbox with wrapping):**
```css
.board-grid {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: var(--spacing-md);
  padding: var(--spacing-md) var(--spacing-lg);
}

.role-card {
  flex: 1 1 14rem;        /* min 14rem, grows equally */
  max-width: 22rem;       /* caps at 22rem max */
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  padding: var(--spacing-md);
  border-radius: 2px;
  background: var(--color-card);
  border: 1px solid var(--color-border);
}
```

**Card States** (visual indicators):
- `.role-card--intel` — Left border 3px primary color (intel only)
- `.role-card--active` — 2px success border + green background tint (has active decision)
- `.role-card--done` — Muted border + 0.7 opacity (submitted)

**Status Badge** (header):
- Displays "INTEL", "DECISION", or "DONE"

**System/Warfare Boards:**
```css
.system-board, .warfare-board {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--spacing-sm);
  padding: var(--spacing-xs) var(--spacing-lg);
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--color-border);
}

.system-board__chips, .warfare-board__chips {
  flex: 1;
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-around;
  gap: var(--spacing-xs);
}
```

---

### 5. CO (COMMANDING OFFICER) VIEW VS CREW VIEWS

**CO View** (when `playerRole === "decision_maker"`):
- Player type: `"decision_maker"`
- Sees: Their own decision card + advisor recommendation cards in the same role card
- Decision form has green border (`.role-card--active`)
- Advisor Recs section shows recommendations from all advisor roles
- Pending recommendations show with dashed border and "pending..." label
- Submitted recommendations show advisor label + their selected option label

**Crew/Advisor Views** (individual advisor role):
- Player type: `"advisor"`
- Sees: Only their own role's card and decisions
- Filtered options: Shows COMMON options (no role) + own-role-specific options
- System picker dropdown appears for options with `targets_system: true`
- No advisor recommendations section (only CO sees that)

**Multi-Role View** (`"all_advisors"`):
- Player type: `"advisor"` (logically, but sees multiple roles)
- Sees: All 3 advisor roles as separate cards simultaneously
- Each advisor card shows independently with its own decision form (if active)
- No CO card or advisor recommendations visible
- Used for 2-player mode where one player is "Crew Members"

---

### 6. 2-PLAYER MODE LAYOUT LOGIC

**File:** `/Users/dragan/Documents/AI-Boilerplate/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/features/waiting-room/two-player-stations.ts`

**Role Assignment for 2-Player:**
```typescript
const TWO_PLAYER_ROLES = [
  { id: "decision_maker", label: "Commanding Officer" },
  { id: "all_advisors", label: "Crew Members" },
];
```

**Game Mode Detection:**
- `gameMode === "simple_collaborative"` (set in exercise.store.ts)
- `playerCountMode` in home-view: `"two_player"` or `"full"` or `"practice"`

**Layout Implications:**
- **Station 1:** One player as `"decision_maker"` (CO) — sees single CO card with advisor recs
- **Station 2:** One player as `"all_advisors"` (Crew) — sees all 3 advisor cards side-by-side
- Same turn events and decisions sync across both views via WebSocket
- Advisors' recommendations appear in real-time in the CO's advisor recs section

**Waiting Room UI:**
- Shows "Scenario stations" (role definitions with player_type badges: CMD/ADV)
- Shows "Crew assignment" section with participant dropdown selectors
- Uses `.crew-station` and `.crew-station__light` for visual status indicators

---

### KEY INSIGHTS

1. **Responsive Card Grid:** Uses `flex: 1 1 14rem` to create responsive card wrapping — cards shrink/grow but maintain minimum 14rem width

2. **Role Filtering Logic:** Three levels of role filtering:
   - Scenario definition (which roles exist)
   - Player assignment (which role(s) this player controls)
   - Decision targeting (which roles see which decisions)

3. **Recommendation Key Format:** Recommendations stored as `"[participantId]:[roleId]"` to support multi-participant advisors; CO extracts role ID for display

4. **Decision Submission Paths:**
   - Advisor: `submitRecommendation()` → backend tracks per-role per-decision
   - CO (decision_maker): `closeEngineDecision()` → closes decision, advances game

5. **Intel Display:** Role-specific intel comes from `event.role_descriptions[roleId]` — allows per-role customization of event context

---

### FILE REFERENCE MAP

**Core Components:**
- Player view: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/features/player/player-view.ts` + `.html`
- Role card: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/features/player/role-card.component.ts`

**Boards:**

- Warfare domains: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/shared/warfare-domain-board.component.ts`

**Styling:**
- Player view CSS: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/shared/components-player-view.css` (497 lines)
- Systems/boards CSS: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/shared/components-systems.css`
- Layout CSS: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/shared/components-exercise-layout.css`

**State Management:**
- Exercise store: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/core/exercise.store.ts`
- Decision API: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/core/decision-api.service.ts`
- Scenario API: `/apps/tfc/frontend/src/app/core/scenario-api.service.ts`

**2-Player Mode:**

**Core challenge:** Presenting massive amounts of data (inventories, skill trees, status, communications) without information overload, while giving players fine control of their environment.

**Key patterns:**

- **Multi-window architecture**: Let players open, close, sort, and rearrange information panels. MMORPGs pioneered this -- players access inventories, skill trees, guild management, and chat simultaneously. The risk is visual clutter when windows overlap and obscure the game view.
- **Hierarchized, customizable UI**: Information must be clear and layered by priority. Let players choose what stays visible vs. what they summon on demand.
- **Contextual information consolidation**: Avoid spreading related information across multiple distinct screen areas. Consolidate contextual data (unit stats, building details, commands) into one or two screen regions -- typically the bottom panel. Splitting attention across top/bottom/sides creates cognitive strain.
- **Magnification on focus**: Highlighted items in lists can be magnified to ease navigation, borrowed from mobile UI conventions applied to same-screen multiplayer.
- **Party management screens**: RPGs use fixed grid layouts with card-like character slots showing key stats (health, class, status) at a glance. The Game UI Database catalogs 55,000+ screenshots across 1,300+ games for reference.

**Reference:** [Game UI Database](https://www.gameuidatabase.com/) for extensive real-world examples of party/team management screens.

---

### 2. Fixed-Size Card Layouts in Game UIs

**Key patterns:**

- **Fixed width + fixed height**: Define a fixed height for cards; use whitespace for cards with less content and truncate text for cards with more. Place cards inside fixed-width columns to keep layout consistent across screen sizes.
- **Grid foundation**: Use a grid system (e.g., 4px or 8px base unit) as the foundation. Grids enforce consistent spacing, margins, and alignment across all cards.
- **Consistent margins within card groups**: Horizontal and vertical spacing between cards must be identical. Follow a clear system (e.g., 4px grid) for padding and margins.
- **Responsive breakpoints**: Create a grid definition for each breakpoint and arrange cards accordingly, so fixed-size cards adapt without breaking layout integrity.
- **Content hierarchy within cards**: Use visual hierarchy -- larger/bolder elements for primary info, smaller fonts for supporting text. Each card should communicate its intent at a glance.

---

### 3. Split-Screen / Panel-Based Game UI for Asymmetric Roles

**The Artemis model** (the gold standard for commander-vs-crew UI):

- **Dedicated station screens**: Each player gets a purpose-built screen for their role:
  - **Helm**: Short-range radar, heading display, speed, energy. Tap-to-steer on radar. Weapon firing arcs overlaid to help align with Weapons officer.
  - **Weapons**: Similar radar layout to Helm but no movement controls -- "riding shotgun." Targeting, beam, and torpedo tube controls.
  - **Engineering**: Power allocation sliders across 8 systems, cooling management, repair team dispatch. A resource management dashboard.
  - **Captain**: No dedicated screen or controls. Decides strategy, relays information between stations, gives orders verbally.
- **Information asymmetry by design**: Each station sees only what it needs. The Helm sees heading/speed/arcs, Weapons sees targeting/ordnance, Engineering sees power/heat/damage. No station has the full picture -- that is the Captain's job to synthesize verbally.
- **Shared controls are minimal**: Only Helm and Weapons can toggle the viewscreen and shields. This prevents conflicts while allowing necessary overlap.

**Other asymmetric patterns found:**

- **Commander/RTS overlay vs. Crew/FPS view** (Savage, Natural Selection): The commander sees a top-down strategic map and issues orders; crew members see first-person with a focused HUD showing only their immediate context.
- **Information advantage asymmetry** (Pac-Man Vs.): The "commander" role gets a full overview; subordinate roles get limited visibility.
- **Captain's chair override** (Shores of Hazeron): The captain's station does little alone but can override any other station when needed.

**Key design principle**: In asymmetric games, the commander needs an **overview dashboard** (map, status summaries of all units/stations), while crew members need **focused, role-specific panels** with only the controls and information relevant to their task.

---

### 4. Game Design Heuristics for Situational Awareness

**Endsley's 3-level situation awareness model applied to games:**
1. **Level 1 -- Perception**: What is happening right now? (status indicators, alerts)
2. **Level 2 -- Comprehension**: What does it mean? (patterns, cause-effect)
3. **Level 3 -- Projection**: What will happen next? (predictive indicators, timers, trends)

Research showed that UI designed around Level 3 SA (showing projections/predictions) significantly improved both task performance and SA scores.

**Practical cognitive load reduction strategies:**

- **Color coding for instant parsing**: Red = danger, green = health/positive, blue = resources. Diablo IV uses green/red for positive/negative item effects.
- **Dynamic HUD elements**: Change color when health is low, flash to indicate danger, pulse for urgency. Information adapts to context rather than being static.
- **Progressive disclosure**: Defer advanced or rarely-used features to secondary screens. Start general, reveal specifics on demand. Use accordions, tabs, and conditional display.
- **Consistent visual language**: Create a design system where patterns are recognizable. Players learn the "vocabulary" once and can read new information faster.
- **"At a glance" principle**: Every UI element should communicate its intent instantly through labels, icons, and colors. If a player has to study an element to understand it, it is too complex for its position in the hierarchy.
- **Consolidate, do not scatter**: Group related information spatially. Having resources at the top, commands at the bottom, and orders on the right forces the eye to jump constantly. Pick one or two anchor zones.

**From Nielsen's 10 heuristics applied to games:**
- Show only context-relevant controls (Red Dead Redemption 2 shows controls only when contextually appropriate in the lower-right).
- Visibility of system status: Always let the player know what is going on through timely feedback.

---

### 5. Dashboard/Cockpit UI Patterns from Simulators and Serious Games

**Artemis / EmptyEpsilon / Thorium Nova design principles:**

- **Role = screen**: Each bridge station is a separate screen/computer. No one sees everything. This enforces communication and teamwork.
- **Engineering as a resource dashboard**: Power sliders for 8 subsystems, heat gauges, coolant allocation, repair team management. This is essentially a real-time dashboard with multiple competing resource meters.
- **Helm as a spatial navigation console**: Radar/map centered, with heading and speed readouts. Weapon arcs overlaid as spatial reference.
- **Information flows through the Captain**: The captain has no screen -- they synthesize verbal reports from all stations. This is a deliberate design choice: the "dashboard" for the commander is the team itself.

**Strategy game dashboard patterns (from Gamedeveloper.com):**

- **Reserve the bottom of screen for contextual info**: Unit stats, building details, commands -- all in one centralized location for quick assessment.
- **Minimap as persistent overview**: Always visible, always updating. Provides spatial awareness without leaving the current view.
- **Picture-in-picture**: Some strategy games show a secondary view (e.g., base status) while the main view is elsewhere.
- **Hotkeys for every command**: The UI should be operable without the mouse for experienced players. Every panel action should have a keyboard shortcut.

**The four types of game UI (Toptal framework):**

| Type | In Game World? | Characters See It? | Example |
|------|---------------|-------------------|---------|
| Non-diegetic | No | No | Health bar, score, ammo counter |
| Diegetic | Yes | Yes | In-cockpit instruments, wrist-mounted device |
| Spatial | Yes | No | Waypoint markers, selection highlights |
| Meta | No (story only) | N/A | Screen blood splatter, vignette effects |

For a commander/crew game, **non-diegetic** UI (HUD overlays, status panels) is the primary pattern for crew stations, while **diegetic** UI (in-world screens, cockpit displays) adds immersion when appropriate.

---

### Summary of Actionable Recommendations

1. **Give each role a dedicated, purpose-built panel** with only the information and controls that role needs. Do not give everyone the same UI with different permissions.
2. **Use fixed-size cards on a grid** for character/unit/role panels. Fixed height with truncation or whitespace. 4px or 8px grid for spacing consistency.
3. **Consolidate information into 1-2 screen zones** rather than scattering across all edges. Bottom panel for contextual detail, persistent mini-overview in a corner.
4. **Apply progressive disclosure**: Show summary state by default, expand to detail on interaction. Accordions and tabs within panels.
5. **Color-code status at a glance**: Use a small, consistent palette (3-5 colors max) for status states (OK, warning, critical, inactive, selected).
6. **The commander gets an overview dashboard** (all units/roles summarized); crew members get focused workstation views.
7. **Design for Level 3 SA**: Show not just current state but trends and predictions (timers, progress bars, directional indicators).
8. **Keep cards/panels at consistent sizes** so the eye can scan predictably. Varying sizes force re-parsing of layout.

## Interface Complexity in Multiplayer RPGs

The complexity of game interfaces in MMORPGs represents a major challenge that distinguishes them from other genres. Unlike FPS games that display limited essential information, MMORPGs must simultaneously manage massive amounts of data, requiring players to access inventories, skill trees, guild management menus, complex economic systems, and branching dialogues.

## Information Architecture Challenges

These elements require an interface that is clear, hierarchized, and customizable to avoid information overload, while still giving players fine control and understanding of their environment. A multi-window architecture allows players greater freedom to access information and manage multiple parameters simultaneously, which is essential for social coordination, planning, and fast-paced combat.

However, this richness introduces visual overload or clutter—when too many windows pile up or overlap, they can obscure the main view and generate visual confusion that penalizes gameplay.

## Design Solutions for Multiple Character Management

Some games offer UI solutions for same-screen multiplayer that bring mobile UI metaphors to allow multiple players to open menus simultaneously with comfort. Highlighted items in lists can be magnified to make navigation easier, while sections of content can be closed, opened, and sorted appropriately.

The search results also show that game UI databases explore over 1,300 games with 55,000 UI screenshots, providing valuable references for character management and team-based UI patterns.

## Key Findings:

**Game Design Heuristics and Cognitive Load**

Jakob Nielsen's 10 heuristics for user-interface design are applicable to video games. A particularly relevant application involves managing information presentation: Red Dead Redemption 2 minimizes cognitive load by presenting context-relevant controls in the lower right area of the screen.

**Situational Awareness and User Interface**

User interface design can be developed based on a three-level situation awareness model, and research has shown that a level-3 interface effectively improved task performance and situation awareness scores in game environments.

**Managing Multiple Information Streams**

Cognitive load in game design refers to the mental effort players must expend to process and understand information, including game mechanics, rules, objectives, goals, controls, and visual and auditory stimuli. When too many elements are presented simultaneously, this can overload a player's working memory causing cognitive overload, making it harder for players to process information and make decisions.

**Practical Strategies**

Board games use various techniques to convey information and reduce cognitive load, including scoring tracks and pawns to mark positioning. Additionally, using visual, auditory, and tactile cues to provide affordances—such as vibrating controllers or items that light up—can provide effective feedback.

I found comprehensive information about fixed size card layout game UI design patterns and consistent panel sizes. Here are the key findings:

## Core Card Design Principles

A "card" is a UI design pattern that groups related information in a flexible-size container visually resembling a playing card. However, for consistent panel sizes specifically, fixing the width of a card keeps the layout of its contents consistent across different screen sizes by placing it inside a column configured with a fixed width.

## Fixed Size Implementation

Define a fixed height for cards by leaving whitespace for cards with less content and making the text truncated when the card has more content. This is a core pattern for maintaining visual consistency.

## Grid-Based Consistency

Grid is a foundation for a card-based layout as they help arrange content consistently, which is why they are so useful when it comes to card design. A grid system helps keep your cards neatly arranged and consistent by ensuring the spacing, margins, and alignment are the same across all your cards.

## Spacing and Margin Guidelines

Use consistent margin dimensions within card groups on a page to achieve a balanced UI, and when displaying multiple cards, make sure that the horizontal and vertical spacing is consistent. Follow a clear system (e.g., a 4px grid) for padding and margins to keep layouts organized and sharp across screens.

## Key Findings

**Progressive Disclosure & Cognitive Load:**

Progressive Disclosure defers advanced or rarely used features to a secondary screen, reducing cognitive load on the current task at hand. Progressive disclosure is a technique UX designers use to reduce cognitive load by gradually revealing more complex information or features as the user progresses through a user interface of a digital product.

**Information Hierarchy & Visual Organization:**

Use visual hierarchy, with larger, bolder elements for key points and smaller fonts for supportive text. Rather than present all information at once, you break it into small bites starting general and moving more specific, either by only displaying one bite at a time or by grouping bites together where information hierarchy makes it easier to scan and process.

**UI Design Patterns:**

Accordions give users control over when and if they need content, particularly helpful when presenting lots of content like FAQs. Tabs allow designers to organize content into categories so users can choose when they need it and reduce scrolling. Dropdown menus help keep UIs uncluttered by hiding long lists, allowing users to focus on the current task without being distracted by irrelevant content.

**Practical Implementation:**

When designing complex forms, show only what's relevant to the current task, and introduce additional fields as users progress, either by breaking a long complex form into multiple pages or implementing conditional logic that displays fields based on previous answers.

## Bridge Station Overview

The game is designed to be played between three and eight players over a local area network, with each player using a separate computer that provides a different spaceship bridge station, such as helm control or engineering.

## Station-Specific UI Designs

**Helm Station:**
In the upper-left corner, the Helms officer's screen displays the ship's energy (max is 1,000), current heading in degrees, and current speed in Units/minute. The Helms officer has a short-range radar. Pressing inside this radar sets the ship's heading in that direction. If the ship has beam weapons, the radar view includes those weapons' firing arcs to help the Helms officer keep targets in the Weapons officer's sights.

**Weapons Station:**
The weapons or tactical officer controls the ship's weapons: targeting, beams, and torpedo tubes. The display is remarkably similar to that of the helm, but you have no control over where you're going. You're essentially riding shotgun for the helm, who is driving.

**Engineering Station:**
The engineer allocates power and cooling to the ship's eight systems, and manages repair teams. Energy is a finite resource which is refilled by docking at a space station, and consumed by any system that's active. Higher power causes a system to perform faster (such as turning and moving faster, loading torpedoes faster, or making shields stronger), but also causes it to generate more heat, and cooling is also a limited resource.

**Captain's Station:**
The captain decides policy and strategy, gives commands to other stations to implement that strategy, and to some degree relays information between stations. The captain does not have a dedicated screen and does not have any controls.

## Screen Sharing Feature

Both Helm and Weapons stations can control the viewscreen and the shields.

## Key Design Patterns

Asymmetric Multiplayer is a multiplayer mode in which the different players have totally different roles and capabilities, unlike most multiplayer games, where all the players are generally doing the same thing and playing the game the same way.

## Commander vs. Crew Example

One player on each team would be the commander and could see the entire battlefield and issue orders to players. All other players would be individual soldiers. This is exemplified in games like Savage: The Battle For Newerth.

In previous games, each team had a 'Commander' role who could use various abilities to impact the flow of the battle: calling in artillery, respawning troops more quickly, etc. With Rising Storm 2, the developers made them wildly different; almost no abilities are shared between forces. Essentially, they wanted the commanders to be playing a strategic sub-game against one another.

## Perspective Differences

As the killer, you can dominate the game from both first and third-person perspectives, gaining tactical advantages, while survivors navigate challenges exclusively in third-person view for a truly immersive struggle. This demonstrates how different perspectives support asymmetric gameplay.

## Crew Station Design

Shores of Hazeron had multiple crew stations on its starships, each of which had unique tasks; the helmsman flew the ship, sensor station locked and scanned targets, and the engineer had to keep multiple constantly moving status indicators for the engines/reactor/FTL drive within a green zone or they would become inefficient, etc. The Captain's chair did little on its own, but could override other stations on the ship.

## Contextual Panels and Information Organization

## Key Strategies for Minimizing Cognitive Overload in Game UI

**Status Indicators & "At a Glance" Information:**
Every element should communicate intent at a glance, with labels, icons, and colors reducing ambiguity. Dynamic HUD elements that change based on player actions or environmental context—such as changing color when health is low or flashing to indicate danger—are critical for providing real-time information.

**Color Coding:**
Different colors can represent various elements — red for danger, green for health, blue for resources — making it easy for players to quickly identify information. Diablo IV highlights the positive and negative effects of items in green and red, providing visual cues to process information.

**Visual Hierarchy:**
Visual hierarchy in gaming UI ensures that players quickly see and understand important information, which is especially critical in high-paced action games where every second counts. Strategies such as visual hierarchy, scaffolding information, and minimizing unnecessary details can help reduce cognitive load.

**Design System Consistency:**
Creating a consistent visual language will help players recognize patterns and make it easier to understand and process the presented information.

**Multiplayer Considerations:**

## Toptal Game UI Guide: Diegetic, Spatial, Meta, and HUD Design Patterns

The Toptal guide "Level Up: A Guide to Game UI" outlines four classes of video game UI components: Non-diegetic; Diegetic; Spatial; and Meta.

### The Four UI Types:

**Non-Diegetic UI**: Non-diegetic UI components reside outside of a game's story and space. None of the characters in the game, including a player's avatar, are aware that the components exist. Non-Diegetic components commonly appear in video games as stat meters. They keep track of points, time, damage, and various resources that players amass and expend during gameplay.

**Diegetic UI**: Diegetic UI components inhabit both a game's story and space, and characters within the game are aware of the components.

**Spatial UI**: Spatial UI components are found in a game's space, but characters within the game don't see them. Spatial components often work as visual aids, helping players select objects or pointing out important landmarks. Text labels are a classic example of spatial UI components. In fantasy and adventure games, players may encounter important objects that are unfamiliar in appearance. Text labels quickly remove ambiguity and keep players immersed in the gaming experience.

**Meta UI**: Meta UI components exist in a game's story, but they don't reside in the game's space.

The guide emphasizes that video game user interface design has a substantial impact on a game's playability and user experience.

content.text: A laptop first. maybe with bigger external monitor

Good — laptop-first with optional large monitor. That means **3 columns side-by-side is viable** and we should scale up gracefully on bigger screens without wasting space.

Next question:

**How should the 3 crew role cards relate to each other visually?** The research strongly suggests two patterns for multi-role management:

- **(A) Equal columns** — all 3 roles get exactly 1/3 of the horizontal space, always. Like Artemis bridge stations — each role is its own "workstation." Content scrolls within its column if needed.
- **(B) Focus + context** — one role is "active/expanded" (e.g., the one with a pending decision) and gets ~50% width, while the other two are compressed to ~25% each showing summary state. Clicking/interacting swaps focus.
- **(C) Tabbed with summary strip** — a persistent summary strip shows all 3 roles' status at a glance, but only one role's full card is shown at a time. Tabs to switch.

My recommendation is **(A) Equal columns** because:
- It matches your constraint of "fixed real estate that doesn't change size"
- The crew player needs to see all 3 roles simultaneously for situational awareness
- It's how Artemis/EmptyEpsilon solve the same problem (each station = fixed viewport)
- No layout shift = lower cognitive load when scanning across roles

Which approach feels right?
A by default and B on demand

content.thinking:
The user wants equal columns by default, with the ability to expand one role on demand. This is a great hybrid approach.

content.text:
Smart hybrid — equal columns as baseline, click-to-focus when you need detail. This gives both scan-ability and drill-down.

Next question:

**Within each column, how should the vertical space be divided?** Each role card currently has variable-height sections (intel, decision form, done state). To keep cards at fixed size, we need a strategy for content that doesn't fit.

The research says: fixed height cards with consistent zones let the eye scan predictably across columns.

- **(A) Fixed vertical zones** — each column is split into 2 stacked zones of fixed height:
  - **Top zone** (~40%): Intel/event inject — always visible, scrolls internally if text overflows
  - **Bottom zone** (~60%): Decision/bluecard form — always occupies this space, shows empty state or "waiting for decision" when no active decision
  
- **(B) Fixed total height, flexible internal split** — column height is locked to viewport, but the intel and decision sections flex based on content (e.g., short intel = more room for decision options)

- **(C) Something else** you had in mind?

My recommendation is **(A)** — it directly satisfies your "same real estate, don't change size" requirement. When the crew player scans left-to-right, intel is always at eye-level in the same row, decisions are always below in the same row. Predictable spatial mapping per Gestalt proximity principle.
A.

Good. Fixed zones, predictable layout.

Next question:

**What should happen when a role is expanded (the "focus" mode from option B)?**

- **(A) Overlay/modal** — the expanded role pops up as a centered overlay on top of the 3-column grid. The grid stays visible underneath (dimmed). Click outside or press Esc to dismiss.
- **(B) Inline expand** — the focused column grows to ~50% width, the other two shrink to ~25% each. Everything stays in the same plane, just resized. Click the role header again to collapse back to equal thirds.
- **(C) Slide-out panel** — the expanded role opens as a side panel (like the existing logs drawer), showing full detail. The 3-column grid stays intact underneath.

My recommendation is **(B) Inline expand** because:
- Maintains spatial position — the expanded role stays "where it was," so the player doesn't lose spatial mapping
- The other two roles remain visible at reduced fidelity (just header + status badge + truncated intel), maintaining situational awareness
- No layer-switching cognitive cost (modals break flow in time-pressured games)
- Smooth CSS transition with `grid-template-columns` animation

Which one?
B

Clean. Inline expand, no context-switching.

Next question:

**What about the turn event banner?** Currently there's a single shared banner at the top showing the turn event title + description. But in the fixed-zone model, each role already has its own intel zone showing role-specific event descriptions.

- **(A) Keep the shared banner** — it shows the global event title/description. Each role's intel zone shows the role-specific description from `role_descriptions[roleId]`. Two levels of info: global context up top, role-specific below.
- **(B) Remove the shared banner** — fold the turn number + event title into each role's intel zone header. Reclaims vertical space for the fixed zones. The event title is the same across all 3 roles anyway, so it's redundant.
- **(C) Collapse the banner to a minimal strip** — just "TURN 3 — Phishing Attack Detected" as a thin bar (one line), no description. Role-specific detail lives in the intel zones.

My recommendation is **(C)** — in a fixed-height layout, every pixel of vertical space matters. A minimal turn strip gives global context (turn number + event name) without eating into the role zones. The detailed description belongs in the per-role intel zones where it can be role-specific anyway.

Which approach?
diff between an A and C ?

The difference:

**A (Full banner):**
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TURN 3   Phishing Attack Detected                       │
│ A sophisticated spear-phishing campaign has been         │
│ detected targeting multiple crew members...              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌─── Role 1 ───┐ ┌─── Role 2 ───┐ ┌─── Role 3 ───┐
│ role-specific │ │ role-specific │ │ role-specific │
│ intel here    │ │ intel here    │ │ intel here    │
```
- ~3-4 lines tall, shows the **generic** event description (same for everyone)
- Role intel zones then show **role-specific** descriptions below
- Potential redundancy: the generic description often overlaps with role-specific ones

**C (Minimal strip):**
```
┌ TURN 3 — Phishing Attack Detected ─────────────────────┐
┌─── Role 1 ───┐ ┌─── Role 2 ───┐ ┌─── Role 3 ───┐
│ role-specific │ │ role-specific │ │ role-specific │
│ intel here    │ │ intel here    │ │ intel here    │
```
- ~1 line tall, just the label — no generic description paragraph
- Saves ~2-3 lines of vertical space for the role zones
- You lose the shared narrative description, but each role's intel zone carries the detail that matters to that role

**Net trade-off:** C gives you ~40-60px more vertical space for the fixed zones. A gives a shared narrative framing that might help the crew player understand the "big picture" before reading role-specific intel. 

Does the generic event description add enough value over the role-specific ones to justify the space?
C: but bigger font size

Got it — minimal strip but prominent. The turn label becomes a strong visual anchor, almost like a chapter heading.

Next question:

**How should the CO (decision maker) view be laid out on their screen?** The CO has a fundamentally different job — they see one role card with advisor recommendations trickling in, then make the final call.

- **(A) Single centered card** — one card in the center of the screen, wider than the crew cards (~50-60% viewport width). Advisor recs stack inside it. Generous whitespace on sides. Simple, focused.
- **(B) Split layout: recommendations left, decision right** — left panel shows the 3 advisor recommendations as they come in (stacked cards, one per advisor). Right panel shows the CO's decision form. Clear separation between "what my crew thinks" and "what I decide."
- **(C) Mirror the crew layout** — 3 small advisor-rec columns on top or left (showing each advisor's status/recommendation), with the CO's decision form below or right. The CO sees the same spatial mapping as the crew — role 1 is always left, role 2 center, role 3 right.

My recommendation is **(C)** because:
- Spatial consistency between screens — if the CO watches the crew's screen, the roles are in the same positions
- The CO's job is to synthesize 3 inputs into one decision — seeing them in the same layout helps pattern-match
- The decision form sits below/beside as a "synthesis zone"

Confirmed — decisions can target the CO directly (`target_roles: ["co", "ops", ...]`), and when `target_roles` is empty, **all** roles see the decision. So the CO has:

1. Their own role-specific intel
2. Their own decision form (when targeted)

So the CO's screen is busier than just "wait for recs, then decide." Let me re-ask:

**CO layout — given they have their own intel + decisions + advisor recs, how should their screen be structured?**

- **(A) Mirror the crew's 3-column layout** — CO sees 3 columns showing each advisor's status/recommendation, plus their own CO card as a wider panel below (or as a 4th column). The CO can see what each crew role is dealing with.
- **(B) Two-zone split** — Left: CO's own card (intel + decision form, ~60% width). Right: stacked advisor recommendation cards (~40% width). The CO's focus is on their own decision, advisor recs are peripheral context.
- **(C) Single column, vertically stacked** — CO intel at top, advisor recs in the middle, CO decision form at bottom. Simple linear flow: read → absorb recs → decide.

My recommendation is **(B)** — the CO's primary job is making decisions, so their card should dominate. Advisor recs are inputs to that decision, not equal peers. This matches the Artemis "captain synthesizes" pattern.

That changes things — if the CO's primary flow is **read recs → pick one → confirm**, then the recommendations are the main content, not peripheral.

Revised options:

- **(A) Recommendations-first layout** — Advisor recs as 3 columns (mirroring the crew's spatial positions) take up the top ~60%. CO's decision form sits below as a full-width "action bar" — essentially a confirmation zone. The CO scans recs left-to-right, then acts below.
- **(B) Recs left, decision right** — 3 stacked advisor recs on the left (~50%), CO decision form on the right (~50%). Side-by-side so the CO can glance left while selecting on the right.

My recommendation is **(A)** because:
- The spatial mapping matches the crew screen — role 1 left, role 2 center, role 3 right on both screens
- The flow is top-down: **absorb → decide** (natural reading order)
- The decision form as a bottom action bar is a well-established "shopping cart checkout" pattern — review items above, commit below
- If someone watches both screens side-by-side, the roles align

A

Great. Recommendations up top mirroring crew positions, decision bar below. Clean top-down flow.

Next question:

**What should each advisor rec column show the CO?** Currently the CO sees just a role label + the selected option (or "pending..."). But since you said the CO mostly follows recommendations, they might need more context to evaluate them.

- **(A) Minimal — just the recommendation** — Role label + what they picked + maybe a confidence indicator. The CO trusts crew and just needs to know "what did they choose?" Fast to scan.
- **(B) Recommendation + role intel summary** — Show a truncated version of the role-specific intel that the advisor saw, plus their pick. The CO can understand *why* the advisor recommended what they did without having to ask.
- **(C) Full mirror** — Show exactly what the crew player sees for that role (intel + decision options with the advisor's pick highlighted). The CO sees the full picture per role.

My recommendation is **(B)** — pure minimal (A) might not give the CO enough to evaluate conflicting recommendations. Full mirror (C) is too dense and duplicates the crew screen. A truncated intel + the pick gives the CO just enough context to make an informed call.

**How should the CO's bottom decision bar work when they're confirming a recommendation?** The CO sees 3 full role mirrors above, then needs to act.

- **(A) Pick-to-confirm** — The CO clicks on one of the advisor's highlighted recommendations directly in the column above, and a confirmation button appears in the bottom bar: "Confirm [Role X]'s recommendation: [Option Y]?" One click to select, one click to confirm.

- **(C) Hybrid** — Bottom bar shows all options. When an advisor submits a rec, their option gets a visual boost (badge: "recommended by OPS"). The CO can pick any option, but recommended ones are visually promoted.

My recommendation is **(C)** — it preserves the CO's autonomy (they can override), while making the common case (follow a rec) easy by promoting recommended options. (A) is too restrictive — what if the CO disagrees? (B) ignores the recommendations entirely in the interaction flow.

## TFC Decision Mechanics - Complete Analysis

Based on my thorough exploration of the codebase, here's how the TFC decision mechanics work:

### 1. **How the CO Closes/Confirms a Decision**

**API Flow:**
- Frontend calls: `DecisionApiService.closeEngineDecision()` → `POST /api/exercises/{exerciseId}/engine/decisions/{decisionId}/close`
- Request body: `{ selected_option_ids: string[], target_system_selections: Record<string, string> }`
- Backend processes via `EngineDecisionService.close_decision()` which delegates to `ExerciseEngine.close_decision()`

**Canonical Close Path** (from `exercise_engine.py:189-268`):
1. Validate decision exists and is open
2. Validate `max_selections` constraint (if template specifies limit)
3. Close the decision in DecisionManager
4. Score using game mode's `on_decision_closed_v2()` method
5. Resolve forced cards (auto-add missing mandatory options)

1→"""Manages in-flight decision points during exercise execution.
     2→
     3→Passive tracker — does not control the engine directly.
     4→The engine checks decision state in its tick loop.
     5→"""
     6→
     7→from __future__ import annotations
     8→
     9→import time as _time_mod
    10→from dataclasses import dataclass, field
    11→
    12→from engine.state_changes import (
    13→    DecisionClosed,
    14→    DecisionOpened,
    15→    DecisionOptionSnapshot,
    16→    DecisionSnapshot,
    17→    RecommendationSubmitted,
    18→)
    19→
    20→
    21→@dataclass
    22→class ActiveDecision:
    23→    """Runtime representation of a decision point."""
    24→
    25→    id: str
    26→    event_id: str | None
    27→    issue_id: str | None
    28→    title: str
    29→    description: str
    30→    question_type: str
    31→    options: list[DecisionOptionSnapshot]
    32→    completion_mode: str
    33→    target_roles: list[str]
    34→    timeout_ms: float = 0.0  # 0 = no timeout
    35→    max_selections: int | None = None  # None = unlimited
    36→    status: str = "open"  # open, closed, timed_out
    37→    opened_at_pt_ms: float = 0.0
    38→    opened_at_rt_ms: float = 0.0  # wall clock for timeout tracking
    39→    closed_at_pt_ms: float | None = None
    40→    recommendations: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    41→    selected_option_ids: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    42→
    43→
    44→class DecisionManager:
    45→    """Tracks active decision requests during an exercise."""
    46→
    47→    def __init__(self) -> None:
    48→        self._decisions: dict[str, ActiveDecision] = {}
    49→
    50→    def open_decision(
    51→        self,
    52→        *,
    53→        id: str,
    54→        event_id: str | None,
    55→        issue_id: str | None,
    56→        title: str,
    57→        description: str,
    58→        question_type: str,
    59→        options: list[DecisionOptionSnapshot],
    60→        completion_mode: str,
    61→        target_roles: list[str],
    62→        timeout_ms: float = 0.0,
    63→        max_selections: int | None = None,
    64→        current_pt_ms: float,
    65→    ) -> DecisionOpened:
    66→        """Register a new open decision. Returns a change dict."""
    67→        decision = ActiveDecision(
    68→            id=id,
    69→            event_id=event_id,
    70→            issue_id=issue_id,
    71→            title=title,
    72→            description=description,
    73→            question_type=question_type,
    74→            options=options,
    75→            completion_mode=completion_mode,
    76→            target_roles=target_roles,
    77→            timeout_ms=timeout_ms,
    78→            max_selections=max_selections,
    79→            status="open",
    80→            opened_at_pt_ms=current_pt_ms,
    81→            opened_at_rt_ms=_time_mod.monotonic() * 1000,
    82→        )
    83→        self._decisions[id] = decision
    84→        return {
    85→            "type": "decision_opened",
    86→            "id": id,
    87→            "decision_id": id,
    88→            "event_id": event_id,
    89→            "issue_id": issue_id,
    90→            "title": title,
    91→            "description": description,
    92→            "question_type": question_type,
    93→            "options": options,
    94→            "completion_mode": completion_mode,
    95→            "target_roles": target_roles,
    96→            "timeout_ms": timeout_ms,
    97→            "max_selections": max_selections,
    98→            "status": "open",
    99→            "opened_at_pt_ms": current_pt_ms,
   100→            "closed_at_pt_ms": None,
   101→            "recommendations": {},
   102→        }
   103→
   104→    def close_decision(
   105→        self,
   106→        decision_id: str,
   107→        *,
   108→        current_pt_ms: float,
   109→        selected_option_ids: list[str] | None = None,
   110→    ) -> DecisionClosed | None:
   111→        """Close a decision. Returns a change dict or None."""
   112→        decision = self._decisions.get(decision_id)
   113→        if decision is None or decision.status == "closed":
   114→            return None
   115→        decision.status = "closed"
   116→        decision.closed_at_pt_ms = current_pt_ms
   117→        decision.selected_option_ids = selected_option_ids or []
   118→        return {
   119→            "type": "decision_closed",
   120→            "decision_id": decision_id,
   121→            "title": decision.title,
   122→            "selected_option_ids": decision.selected_option_ids,
   123→        }
   124→
   125→    def tick(self, current_pt_ms: float) -> list[DecisionClosed]:
   126→        """Check open decisions for timeout expiry. Returns changes."""
   127→        changes: list[DecisionClosed] = []
   128→        for d in self._decisions.values():
   129→            if d.status != "open" or d.timeout_ms <= 0:
   130→                continue
   131→            elapsed = current_pt_ms - d.opened_at_pt_ms
   132→            if elapsed >= d.timeout_ms:
   133→                d.status = "timed_out"
   134→                d.closed_at_pt_ms = current_pt_ms
   135→                changes.append(
   136→                    {
   137→                        "type": "decision_closed",
   138→                        "decision_id": d.id,
   139→                        "title": d.title,
   140→                    }
   141→                )
   142→        return changes
   143→
   144→    def submit_recommendation(
   145→        self,
   146→        decision_id: str,
   147→        participant_id: str,
   148→        option_id: str,
   149→        role_id: str | None = None,
   150→    ) -> RecommendationSubmitted | None:
   151→        """Record an advisor's recommendation. Returns a change dict or None.
   152→
   153→        When *role_id* is provided the recommendation is keyed as
   154→        ``participant_id:role_id`` so that a single participant can submit
   155→        one recommendation per role (used by the all-advisors 2-player mode).
   156→        """
   157→        decision = self._decisions.get(decision_id)
   158→        if decision is None or decision.status != "open":
   159→            return None
   160→        key = f"{participant_id}:{role_id}" if role_id else participant_id
   161→        decision.recommendations[key] = option_id
   162→        return {
   163→            "type": "recommendation_submitted",
   164→            "decision_id": decision_id,
   165→            "participant_id": key,
   166→            "option_id": option_id,
   167→        }
   168→
   169→    def get_decision(self, decision_id: str) -> ActiveDecision | None:
   170→        """Look up a decision by ID, regardless of status."""
   171→        return self._decisions.get(decision_id)
   172→
   173→    def get_open_decisions(self) -> list[ActiveDecision]:
   174→        """Return only decisions with status 'open'."""
   175→        return [d for d in self._decisions.values() if d.status == "open"]
   176→
   177→    def snapshot(self) -> list[DecisionSnapshot]:
   178→        """Return all decisions as serializable dicts."""
   179→        return [
   180→            DecisionSnapshot(
   181→                id=d.id,
   182→                event_id=d.event_id,
   183→                issue_id=d.issue_id,
   184→                title=d.title,
   185→                description=d.description,
   186→                question_type=d.question_type,
   187→                options=d.options,
   188→                completion_mode=d.completion_mode,
   189→                target_roles=d.target_roles,
   190→                timeout_ms=d.timeout_ms,
   191→                max_selections=d.max_selections,
   192→                status=d.status,
   193→                opened_at_pt_ms=d.opened_at_pt_ms,
   194→                closed_at_pt_ms=d.closed_at_pt_ms,
   195→                recommendations=dict(d.recommendations),
   196→                selected_option_ids=list(d.selected_option_ids),
   197→            )
   198→            for d in self._decisions.values()
   199→        ]
   200→
   201→    def clear(self) -> None:

1→"""Simple-Collaborative game mode.
     2→
     3→No GM required. Decisions chain sequentially — each opens immediately
     4→when the previous one closes. Advisors submit recommendations in
     5→real-time; the decision-maker makes the final call. Wrong answers
     6→increase stress, which reduces the time available for subsequent decisions.
     7→"""
     8→
     9→from __future__ import annotations
    10→
    11→from dataclasses import dataclass, field
    12→
    13→from engine.state_changes import DecisionOptionSnapshot, ForcedCardApplied, ScoreChange, StateChange
    14→
    15→STRESS_TIME_TABLE: dict[int, int] = {
    16→    0: 300_000,
    17→    1: 290_000,
    18→    2: 280_000,
    19→    3: 270_000,
    20→    4: 260_000,
    21→    5: 250_000,
    22→    6: 240_000,
    23→    7: 230_000,
    24→    8: 210_000,
    25→    9: 190_000,
    26→    10: 180_000,
    27→}
    28→
    29→
    30→@dataclass
    31→class SimpleCollaborativeMode:
    32→    """Strategy for the simple-collaborative exercise mode."""
    33→
    34→    decision_sequence: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    35→    base_decision_time_ms: int = 300_000
    36→    max_possible_score: float = 0.0
    37→    score_tier_thresholds: dict[str, float] = field(default_factory=dict)
    38→
    39→    # Mutable runtime state
    40→    stress: int = 0
    41→    total_score: float = 0.0
    42→    turn_number: int = 1
    43→    current_index: int = 0
    44→
    45→    def should_pause_on_decision(self) -> bool:
    46→        return False
    47→
    48→    def on_decision_timeout(
    49→        self,
    50→        decision_id: str,
    51→        options: list[DecisionOptionSnapshot],
    52→    ) -> str | None:
    53→        """Auto-submit the worst option (lowest score)."""
    54→        if not options:
    55→            return None
    56→        worst = min(options, key=lambda o: o.get("score", 0))
    57→        return worst["id"]
    58→
    59→    def on_decision_closed_v2(
    60→        self,
    61→        decision_id: str,
    62→        selected_options: list[DecisionOptionSnapshot],
    63→        all_options: list[DecisionOptionSnapshot],
    64→        forced_option_ids: list[str] | None = None,
    65→        turn_stress_delta: int = 0,
    66→    ) -> list[StateChange]:
    67→        """Score using full option lists. Enforces forced cards."""
    68→        changes: list[StateChange] = []
    69→        forced_ids = forced_option_ids or []
    70→
    71→        # Check forced cards — auto-add if missing
    72→        selected_ids = {o["id"] for o in selected_options}
    73→        effective_options = list(selected_options)
    74→        for fid in forced_ids:
    75→            if fid not in selected_ids:
    76→                forced_opt = next(
    77→                    (o for o in all_options if o["id"] == fid),
    78→                    None,
    79→                )
    80→                if forced_opt is not None:
    81→                    effective_options.append(forced_opt)
    82→                    change: ForcedCardApplied = {
    83→                        "type": "forced_card_applied",
    84→                        "decision_id": decision_id,
    85→                        "forced_option_id": fid,
    86→                        "reason": (
    87→                            f"Mandatory card {fid} was not selected and has been auto-applied."
    88→                        ),
    89→                    }
    90→                    changes.append(change)

   189→    async def close_decision(
   190→        self,
   191→        decision_id: str,
   192→        selected_option_ids: list[str],
   193→        target_system_selections: dict[str, str] | None = None,
   194→    ) -> list[StateChange]:
   195→        """Single canonical path for closing a decision.
   196→
   197→        Handles: validate → close → score → resolve forced cards →
   198→        record plays → system effects (with optional target overrides) →
   199→        advance turn → auto-complete.
   200→
   201→        Args:
   202→            target_system_selections: map of option_id → system_id for
   203→                options with targets_system=True. Pass None on timeout
   204→                to skip target-system effects.
   205→
   206→        Raises ValueError if decision missing/closed, max_selections
   207→        violated, or a required target system selection is missing/invalid.
   208→        """
   209→        pt = self._time.play_time_ms
   210→
   211→        decision = self._decisions.get_decision(decision_id)
   212→        if decision is None or decision.status != "open":
   213→            raise ValueError(f"Decision {decision_id} not found or already closed")
   214→
   215→        template = self.find_decision_template(decision_id)
   216→
   217→        # Validate max_selections
   218→        if template and template.max_selections is not None:
   219→            if len(selected_option_ids) > template.max_selections:
   220→                raise ValueError(
   221→                    f"Decision {decision_id} allows at most "
   222→                    f"{template.max_selections} selections, "
   223→                    f"got {len(selected_option_ids)}"
   224→                )
   225→
   226→        # 1. Close
   227→        close_change = self._decisions.close_decision(
   228→            decision_id,
   229→            current_pt_ms=pt,
   230→            selected_option_ids=selected_option_ids,
   231→        )
   232→        if not close_change:
   233→            raise ValueError(f"Decision {decision_id} not found or already closed")
   234→        changes: list[StateChange] = [close_change]
   235→
   236→        # 2. Score (forced cards handled inside game mode)
   237→        selected_opts = [o for o in decision.options if o["id"] in selected_option_ids]
   238→        forced_ids = template.forced_option_ids if template else []
   239→        score_changes = self._config.game_mode.on_decision_closed_v2(
   240→            decision_id,
   241→            selected_opts,
   242→            decision.options,
   243→            forced_option_ids=forced_ids or None,
   244→            turn_stress_delta=template.stress_delta if template else 0,
   245→        )
   246→        changes.extend(score_changes)
   247→
   248→        # 3. Resolve effective options (selected + auto-added forced cards)
   249→        effective_opts = self._resolve_effective_options(
   250→            selected_opts,
   251→            decision.options,
   252→            forced_ids,
   253→        )
   254→
   255→        # 4. Record plays + system effects on effective options
   256→        self.record_option_plays(effective_opts)
   257→        changes.extend(self._apply_system_effects(effective_opts, target_system_selections))
   258→
   259→        # 5. Advance to next turn (or auto-complete if exhausted)
   260→        advance = await self._advance_to_next_turn(decision_id, pt)
   261→        changes.extend(advance)
   262→
   263→        # 6. Auto-resume for GM mode
   264→        if self._config.game_mode.requires_gm():
   265→            if not self._decisions.get_open_decisions():
   266→                changes.append(await self.resume())
   267→
   268→        return changes

    98→        )
    99→    content = ScenarioContent.model_validate(scenario.content)
   100→    return build_engine_config(

   109→async def start_engine(
   110→    exercise_id: int,
   111→    service: ExerciseService = Depends(get_exercise_service),
   112→    scenario_service: ScenarioService = Depends(get_scenario_service),
   113→) -> PhaseChange:
   114→    engine = session_store.get(exercise_id)
   115→    if engine is None:
   116→        exercise = await service.get_exercise(exercise_id)
   117→        config = await _build_config(exercise, scenario_service)
   118→
   119→        async def _on_change(changes: list[StateChange]) -> None:
   120→            await broadcast_changes(connection_manager, exercise_id, changes)
   121→            await _log_to_audit(exercise_id, changes)
   122→
   123→        engine = session_store.create(config, on_state_change=_on_change)
   124→
   125→    # Idempotent: if already in briefing or running, return current phase
   126→    if engine.phase in {EnginePhase.BRIEFING, EnginePhase.RUNNING}:
   127→        return engine._phase_change("started")
   128→
   129→    try:
   130→        result = await engine.start()
   131→    except EngineStateError as exc:
   132→        raise HTTPException(status_code=status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT, detail=str(exc)) from exc
   133→
   134→    await _log_to_audit(exercise_id, [result])
   135→
   136→    # Notify all WS clients so lobby players auto-navigate
   137→    participants = waiting_room_store.list_participants(exercise_id)
   138→    await connection_manager.broadcast(
   139→        exercise_id,
   140→        {
   141→            "type": "exercise_started",
   142→            "exercise_id": exercise_id,
   143→            "participants": [p.to_dict() for p in participants],
   144→        },
   145→    )
   146→    return result

# TFC Two-Player Layout Redesign

## Problem

In 2-player mode (CO + all_advisors), the crew player's 3 role cards use a flex-wrap layout where cards resize based on content. Events/injects and decisions/bluecards change size depending on state, causing layout shift and making it hard to scan across roles predictably.

## Design Decisions

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|----------|----------|
| 1 | Target screen | Laptop-first (1280+), scales to larger monitors |
| 2 | Column layout | Equal thirds by default, inline expand on demand |
| 3 | Vertical zones | Fixed: intel ~40%, decision ~60% of column height |
| 4 | Focus mode | Inline expand: clicked column → 2fr, others → 0.5fr |
| 5 | Turn banner | Minimal 1-line strip, bigger font. No description paragraph |
| 6 | CO view | 3-column mirror of crew + bottom decision bar |
| 7 | CO rec display | Full mirror — CO sees exactly what each crew role sees |
| 8 | CO decision bar | Hybrid — all options shown, recommended ones get advisor badges |
| 9 | Systems/warfare boards | Shared strips above columns (not role-specific) |
| 10 | Stress bar | Stays in header |

## Crew Player Screen (all_advisors)

```

│ HEADER: Title ──── [████ Stress Bar ████] ──── RT / Turn   │
```

### Key rules

## CO (Decision Maker) Screen

```

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key rules

- Top 3 columns = full mirror of crew roles (intel + decision options), read-only
- When advisor submits: their pick highlighted (green border + checkmark)
- "pending..." for advisors who haven't submitted yet
- CO Decision Bar = full-width bottom strip with all decision options
- Recommended options get badges: "★ OPS, PWO"
- CO picks option(s) then clicks Confirm
- No active decision: bar shows "Waiting for next decision..." (muted)
- CO's own intel (from `role_descriptions[co_role_id]`) shown as callout above decision bar

## Interaction States

### Card states (both screens)

| State | Intel Zone | Decision Zone |
|-------|-----------|---------------|
| No event, no decision | "Waiting for next turn..." (muted) | "No active decision" (muted) |
| Event only (intel) | Role-specific description | "No active decision" (muted) |
| Event + active decision | Role-specific description | Options + submit button |
| Decision submitted (done) | Role-specific description | "Selected: [option]" + muted opacity |

Both zones maintain fixed height in ALL states. Empty/waiting states use centered muted text.

### Focus mode columns (crew screen)

| Element | Expanded column (2fr) | Shrunk columns (0.5fr) |
|---------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Role header | Full: ID + label + badge | Compact: ID + badge only |
| Intel zone | Full text, scrollable | Single line, truncated + ellipsis |
| Decision zone | Full options + submit | Status badge only: "DECISION" or "DONE ✓" |

### CO mirror columns

- Read-only — no radio buttons, no submit button
- Options listed as plain text, not interactive
- Advisor pick: `role-card__option--selected` styling + checkmark
- Unpicked options muted
- "pending..." in decision zone header until advisor submits

## Responsive Scaling

| Breakpoint | Behavior |
|-----------|----------|
| 1280–1440px (laptop) | 3 equal columns, comfortable spacing |
| 1920px+ (monitor) | Columns capped ~500px each, centered with margin auto |
| 1024–1280px (narrow) | Columns compress, font sizes step down one tier, chips may wrap |
| <1024px (fallback) | Tabbed view — one role at a time + tab strip |

## CSS Architecture

```css
/* Crew screen: 3 equal columns */
.board-columns {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;
  gap: var(--spacing-md);
  flex: 1;
  min-height: 0;
}

/* Focus mode via data attribute */
.board-columns[data-focus="0"] { grid-template-columns: 2fr 0.5fr 0.5fr; }
.board-columns[data-focus="1"] { grid-template-columns: 0.5fr 2fr 0.5fr; }
.board-columns[data-focus="2"] { grid-template-columns: 0.5fr 0.5fr 2fr; }

/* Each column: fixed vertical zones */
.board-column {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: auto 2fr 3fr; /* header | intel ~40% | decision ~60% */
  min-height: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
  border: 1px solid var(--color-border);
  border-radius: 2px;
  background: var(--color-card);
  transition: grid-template-columns 200ms ease;
}

/* Fixed zones scroll internally */
.board-column__intel,
.board-column__decision {
  overflow-y: auto;
  padding: var(--spacing-md);
}

/* CO decision bar */
.co-decision-bar {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--spacing-md);
  padding: var(--spacing-md) var(--spacing-lg);
  border-top: 2px solid var(--color-success);
  background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--color-success) 5%, var(--color-card));
}

.co-decision-bar__option {
  flex: 1 1 0;
}

.co-decision-bar__option[data-recommended] {
  border-color: var(--color-primary);
  box-shadow: var(--glow-sm);
}
```

## Component Changes

| Component | Change |
|-----------|--------|
| `player-view.ts` | Detect `isDecisionMaker` vs `isAllAdvisors`, render different layouts |
| `board-column.component.ts` (new) | Wraps role content in fixed-zone column, handles focus click |
| `co-decision-bar.component.ts` (new) | Horizontal option picker with recommendation badges |
| `role-card.component.ts` | Add `readonly` input for CO mirror mode (hide submit, show advisor pick) |
| CSS | New `.board-columns` grid replaces `.board-grid` flexbox |

## Game Mechanics Compliance

Verified against backend implementation:

- CO can pick ANY option — not restricted to recommended ones ✓
- Recommendations are purely informational (separate API flow) ✓
- `max_selections` is the only constraint on CO picks ✓
- `completion_mode` field exists but is not currently enforced ✓
- The hybrid decision bar (all options + recommendation badges) preserves full CO autonomy ✓

## Research Backing

Design informed by:

- **Artemis/EmptyEpsilon bridge simulator pattern**: each role = dedicated station screen, captain synthesizes
- **Endsley's 3-level SA model**: perception (status chips), comprehension (role intel), projection (decision options)
- **Gestalt proximity principle**: spatial consistency between CO and crew screens for role positions
- **Fixed-size card best practices**: 4/8px grid, fixed height zones with internal scroll, consistent margins
- **Progressive disclosure**: equal columns by default, expand on demand for detail
- **Nielsen's heuristics**: visibility of system status (badges), consistency (mirrored layouts), user control (focus mode)

```css
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;
  gap: var(--spacing-md);
  flex: 1;
  min-height: 0;
}

/* Focus mode via data attribute */
.board-columns[data-focus="0"] { grid-template-columns: 2fr 0.5fr 0.5fr; }
.board-columns[data-focus="1"] { grid-template-columns: 0.5fr 2fr 0.5fr; }
.board-columns[data-focus="2"] { grid-template-columns: 0.5fr 0.5fr 2fr; }

/* Each column: fixed vertical zones */
.board-column {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: auto 2fr 3fr; /* header | intel ~40% | decision ~60% */
  min-height: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
  border: 1px solid var(--color-border);
  border-radius: 2px;
  background: var(--color-card);
  transition: grid-template-columns 200ms ease;
}

/* Fixed zones scroll internally */
.board-column__intel,
.board-column__decision {
  overflow-y: auto;
  padding: var(--spacing-md);
}

/* CO decision bar */
.co-decision-bar {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--spacing-md);
  padding: var(--spacing-md) var(--spacing-lg);
  border-top: 2px solid var(--color-success);
  background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--color-success) 5%, var(--color-card));
}

.co-decision-bar__option {
  flex: 1 1 0;
}

.co-decision-bar__option[data-recommended] {
  border-color: var(--color-primary);
  box-shadow: var(--glow-sm);
}
```

## Component Changes

| Component | Change |
|-----------|--------|
| `player-view.ts` | Detect `isDecisionMaker` vs `isAllAdvisors`, render different layouts |
| `board-column.component.ts` (new) | Wraps role content in fixed-zone column, handles focus click |
| `co-decision-bar.component.ts` (new) | Horizontal option picker with recommendation badges |
| `role-card.component.ts` | Add `readonly` input for CO mirror mode (hide submit, show advisor pick) |
| CSS | New `.board-columns` grid replaces `.board-grid` flexbox |

## Game Mechanics Compliance

Verified against backend implementation:

- CO can pick ANY option — not restricted to recommended ones ✓
- Recommendations are purely informational (separate API flow) ✓
- `max_selections` is the only constraint on CO picks ✓
- `completion_mode` field exists but is not currently enforced ✓
- The hybrid decision bar (all options + recommendation badges) preserves full CO autonomy ✓

## Research Backing

Design informed by:

- **Artemis/EmptyEpsilon bridge simulator pattern**: each role = dedicated station screen, captain synthesizes
- **Endsley's 3-level SA model**: perception (status chips), comprehension (role intel), projection (decision options)
- **Gestalt proximity principle**: spatial consistency between CO and crew screens for role positions
- **Fixed-size card best practices**: 4/8px grid, fixed height zones with internal scroll, consistent margins
- **Progressive disclosure**: equal columns by default, expand on demand for detail
- **Nielsen's heuristics**: visibility of system status (badges), consistency (mirrored layouts), user control (focus mode)

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md

```bash
grep -i "worktree.*director" CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null
```

**If preference specified:** Use it without asking.

### 3. Ask User

If no directory exists and no CLAUDE.md preference:

```
No worktree directory found. Where should I create worktrees?

1. .worktrees/ (project-local, hidden)
2. ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/<project-name>/ (global location)

Which would you prefer?
```

## Safety Verification

### For Project-Local Directories (.worktrees or worktrees)

**MUST verify .gitignore before creating worktree:**

```bash
# Check if directory pattern in .gitignore
grep -q "^\.worktrees/$" .gitignore || grep -q "^worktrees/$" .gitignore
```

**If NOT in .gitignore:**

Per Jesse's rule "Fix broken things immediately":
1. Add appropriate line to .gitignore
2. Commit the change
3. Proceed with worktree creation

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

### For Global Directory (~/.config/superpowers/worktrees)

No .gitignore verification needed - outside project entirely.

## Creation Steps

### 1. Detect Project Name

```bash
project=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
```

### 2. Create Worktree

```bash
# Determine full path
case $LOCATION in
  .worktrees|worktrees)
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
  ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/*)
    path="~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/$project/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
esac

# Create worktree with new branch
git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

### 3. Run Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

### 4. Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure worktree starts clean:

```bash
# Examples - use project-appropriate command
npm test
cargo test
pytest
go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### 5. Report Location

```
Worktree ready at <full-path>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify .gitignore) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify .gitignore) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Neither exists | Check CLAUDE.md → Ask user |
| Directory not in .gitignore | Add it immediately + commit |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Mistakes

**Skipping .gitignore verification**
- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status
- **Fix:** Always grep .gitignore before creating project-local worktree

**Assuming directory location**
- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions
- **Fix:** Follow priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask

**Proceeding with failing tests**
- **Problem:** Can't distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues
- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed

**Hardcoding setup commands**
- **Problem:** Breaks on projects using different tools
- **Fix:** Auto-detect from project files (package.json, etc.)

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace.

[Check .worktrees/ - exists]
[Verify .gitignore - contains .worktrees/]
[Create worktree: git worktree add .worktrees/auth -b feature/auth]
[Run npm install]
[Run npm test - 47 passing]

Worktree ready at /Users/jesse/myproject/.worktrees/auth
Tests passing (47 tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement auth feature
```

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Create worktree without .gitignore verification (project-local)
- Skip baseline test verification
- Proceed with failing tests without asking
- Assume directory location when ambiguous
- Skip CLAUDE.md check

**Always:**
- Follow directory priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask
- Verify .gitignore for project-local
- Auto-detect and run project setup
- Verify clean test baseline

## Integration

**Called by:**
- **brainstorming** (Phase 4) - REQUIRED when design is approved and implementation follows
- Any skill needing isolated workspace

**Pairs with:**
- **finishing-a-development-branch** - REQUIRED for cleanup after work complete
- **executing-plans** or **subagent-driven-development** - Work happens in this worktree
